Both possible alternating-weight patterns were examined.
For each weight w from 2 through 9 and every allowed adjacent index i (3 ≤ i ≤ 10), the checksum condition (Σ+checksum) ≡ 0 (mod 10) was checked after undoing the swap.
Pattern 1 w 1 w… (even indices weight 1) was already ruled out by previous searches.
For the complementary pattern w 1 w 1… (even indices weight w) a full congruence analysis was carried out:
• For i = 3,4,5,6,7,8,9,10 no single weight satisfied all ten numbers.
• Indices 5 and 6 are impossible because at least one number has d = 0 yet e ≠ 0.
• The remaining indices yield contradictory conditions on w (e.g., k ≡ 4,6,8 simultaneously), so no common w exists.
Consequently there is no weight–index pair that makes all ten numbers valid.

Compute for each candidate adjacent swap index i (3–10) and weight w (2–9).
For each number, let A be the sum of even-index digits (mod 10), B the sum of odd-index digits (mod 10), c the checksum digit.  After swapping digits at i and i+1 the validity condition is
A + c − s + w(B + s) ≡ 0 (mod 10),  where s = sign·(a−b) and sign = +1 if i even, −1 if i odd.
This yields linear congruence (B+s)w ≡ −(A + c − s) (mod 10) that must hold for all ten numbers.
Evaluating each i:
i=3,4,5,6,7,8,10 – no single w satisfies all equations.
For i=9 (columns 9 & 10 swapped) the equations for the ten numbers reduce to
2w≡4, 8w≡6, 3w≡1, 1w≡7, 6w≡2, 6w≡2, 3w≡1, 7w≡9, 4w≡8, 7w≡9 (mod 10),
which are all simultaneously satisfied only by w=7.
Thus the unique solution is weight 7 with the swap starting at index 9.
